label: Blender
blurb: Model game-ready 3D props in Blender and export them clean for Meta Horizon Worlds.

lessons.title: The Blender Window
lessons.subtitle: Where everything lives on screen
steps: The big center area is the 3D Viewport. Your model lives here.
Top right is the Outliner: a list of every object in the scene.
Bottom right is Properties: settings for the selected object.
The bar along the bottom is the Timeline for animation.
Press T for the left tool shelf, N for the right side panel.
lessons.tip: Pro tip: Workspace tabs at the very top (Layout, Modeling, UV) rearrange the screen for you.

quiz.q: Which editor lists every object in your scene?

lessons.title: Moving Around The Viewport
lessons.subtitle: Orbit, pan, zoom and snap views
steps: Hold the middle mouse button and drag to orbit around your model.
Hold Shift and the middle mouse button to pan, or slide the view.
Scroll the wheel to zoom in and out. Ctrl and drag also zooms.
Numpad 1 is front, 3 is right side, 7 is top. Ctrl flips to the back.
Numpad 5 switches between perspective and flat ortho view.
No numpad? Turn on Emulate Numpad in Preferences, Input.
lessons.tip: Pro tip: Press Numpad . (period) to zoom straight to whatever you have selected.

quiz.q: Which numpad key shows the front view?

lessons.title: Move, Rotate And Scale
lessons.subtitle: The three transform tools
steps: Left-click an object to select it. It gets a highlighted outline.
Press G to grab and move. Move the mouse, then click to drop it.
Press R to rotate. Press S to scale bigger or smaller.
After G, R or S, tap X, Y or Z to lock to one axis.
Type a number to be exact, like G Z 2 to move up 2 meters.
Press Esc or right-click to cancel a move partway through.
lessons.tip: Pro tip: The colored arrows and rings (the gizmo) do the same jobs with the mouse.

quiz.q: Which key grabs and moves an object?

lessons.title: The 3D Cursor And Pivot
lessons.subtitle: Where new objects appear
steps: The 3D cursor is the red-white ring. New objects are born at it.
Shift and right-click places the 3D cursor where you point.
Press Shift C to send the cursor back to the world center.
The pivot point is what rotate and scale turn around.
Press the period key to pick a pivot, like Median or 3D Cursor.
lessons.tip: Pro tip: Shift S opens the Snap menu to jump the cursor or object to exact spots.

quiz.q: Where do newly added objects appear?

lessons.title: Adding Objects
lessons.subtitle: The Add menu and mesh shapes
steps: Press Shift A, or click the Add menu in the top bar.
Open Mesh to see starter shapes: Cube, Sphere, Cylinder, Plane.
Click a shape. It drops into the scene at the 3D cursor.
A small panel opens at the bottom left. Click it to set size or cuts.
That panel only works right after adding. It closes once you do more.
lessons.tip: Pro tip: Press F9 to reopen the last add panel if you clicked away too soon.

quiz.q: What shortcut opens the Add menu?

lessons.title: Edit Mode And Object Mode
lessons.subtitle: Tab toggles between the two
steps: Object Mode moves, rotates and scales a whole object at once.
Edit Mode changes the shape by moving its points and faces.
Press Tab to switch between the two modes.
In Edit Mode press 1 for vertices, 2 for edges, 3 for faces.
Vertices are points, edges are lines, faces are flat surfaces.
lessons.tip: Pro tip: Drop back to Object Mode before you move or export the whole object.

quiz.q: Which key switches between Object and Edit Mode?

lessons.title: Essential Edit Tools
lessons.subtitle: Extrude, inset, loop cut and more
steps: In Edit Mode, press E to extrude: pull new geometry out of a face.
Press I to inset: make a smaller face inside the one you have.
Press Ctrl R to add a loop cut: a new ring of edges around the mesh.
Press Ctrl B to bevel an edge into a rounded or chamfered corner.
Press K for the knife to cut your own custom lines across faces.
lessons.tip: Pro tip: While loop cutting, scroll the wheel to add more than one cut at a time.

quiz.q: Which shortcut adds a loop cut?

lessons.title: Modifiers That Save Time
lessons.subtitle: Mirror, subdivide and solidify
steps: Modifiers change your mesh without touching the real points.
Find them under the wrench icon in the Properties editor.
Mirror builds the other half for you. Model once, get both sides.
Subdivision Surface smooths a blocky mesh into soft curves.
Solidify gives a flat surface real thickness, like a wall or a cup.
Apply a modifier to bake it in before you export to Horizon.
lessons.tip: Pro tip: Keep modifiers until the end. They stay editable so you can change your mind.

quiz.q: Which modifier builds the second half of a symmetric model?

lessons.title: Materials Basics
lessons.subtitle: Color, metallic and roughness
steps: A material gives a surface color and shine. Use the Principled BSDF.
Base Color is the plain color of the surface.
Metallic near 0 is plastic or wood. Near 1 is bare metal.
Roughness near 0 is shiny and mirror-like. Near 1 is matte and dull.
Horizon has no normal maps, so bake bumps into the Base Color.
lessons.tip: Pro tip: Horizon reads base color, metallic and roughness. Paint fine detail into the color.

quiz.q: A roughness value near 0 makes a surface look how?

lessons.title: UV Unwrapping
lessons.subtitle: Flatten a mesh for textures
steps: A UV map flattens your 3D surface so a 2D image can wrap onto it.
In Edit Mode, select the edges where the mesh should split open.
Press Ctrl E and choose Mark Seam. Seams act like scissor cuts.
Select everything with A, then press U and choose Unwrap.
Open the UV Editor to see the flat pieces laid out on the texture.
lessons.tip: Pro tip: Good seams hide in corners and creases so the texture has no ugly stretch.

quiz.q: What does marking a seam do before unwrapping?
choices: Tells Blender where to cut open

lessons.title: Bake Detail Into Color
lessons.subtitle: Fake bumps with no normal map
steps: Horizon has no normal maps, so painted-in shading must do the work.
Baking copies light, shadow and bumps onto a flat color image.
Make a new image, select it in the material, and bake in Cycles.
Bake ambient occlusion or detail, then combine it into Base Color.
Now a simple low-poly mesh looks like it has carved detail.
lessons.tip: Pro tip: Bake soft shadows into the color map to fake depth Horizon cannot show otherwise.

quiz.q: Why bake detail into the Base Color for Horizon?
choices: Horizon does not use normal maps

lessons.title: Apply Scale And Rotation
lessons.subtitle: Reset to clean values for export
steps: Blender works in meters. Build your model at real-world size.
After scaling in Object Mode, the Scale value is no longer 1.0.
Odd scale breaks modifiers, physics and the Horizon export.
Press Ctrl A and choose Scale, or All Transforms, to reset to 1.0.
Check the N panel: Scale should read 1.0 on X, Y and Z before export.
lessons.tip: Pro tip: Apply Rotation too so your object points the way Horizon expects when placed.

quiz.q: What should Scale read after you apply it?

lessons.title: The N Panel
lessons.subtitle: Exact location, rotation and size
steps: Press N in the viewport to open the side panel on the right.
The Item tab shows Location, Rotation, Scale and Dimensions.
Type exact numbers here instead of dragging with the mouse.
Dimensions show real size in meters, handy for matching props.
Press N again to hide the panel and free up screen space.
lessons.tip: Pro tip: Set Dimensions directly to size a door or table to the exact meters you need.

quiz.q: Which key opens the N side panel?

lessons.title: Parenting And Collections
lessons.subtitle: Keep a big scene organized
steps: Parenting links objects so the child follows the parent when it moves.
Select the child first, then shift-click the parent, then press Ctrl P.
Collections are folders in the Outliner that group related objects.
Press M to move selected objects into a collection.
Good names and groups make a big build easy to find and select.
lessons.tip: Pro tip: Parent small parts to a main body so the whole thing moves as one in Horizon.

quiz.q: Which key parents the selected objects?

lessons.title: Bones And Weight Paint
lessons.subtitle: Rig a simple model to bend
steps: An armature is a skeleton of bones that make a mesh bend and pose.
Add one with Shift A, Armature. Extrude bones with E in Edit Mode.
Select the mesh, then the armature, and press Ctrl P.
Choose With Automatic Weights so bones grab the nearby surface.
Weight Paint mode shows red for strong pull and blue for none.
Fix spots where a bone bends the wrong part of the mesh.
lessons.tip: Pro tip: Keep rigs simple. A few clean bones animate and export far better than many.

quiz.q: What does Weight Paint control?
choices: How strongly a bone moves a part

lessons.title: Keyframe Animation
lessons.subtitle: Make an object move over time
steps: A keyframe stores a pose at one moment on the timeline.
Go to frame 1, pose the object, then press I to insert a key.
Jump ahead to a later frame, move the object, and press I again.
Blender fills the frames between so the motion plays smoothly.
Press Spacebar to play the animation and watch it loop.
lessons.tip: Pro tip: For Horizon, keep a clean looping action so the motion repeats with no jump.

quiz.q: Which key inserts a keyframe?

lessons.title: Keep Triangle Counts Low
lessons.subtitle: Fast models run well in Horizon
steps: Every face is split into triangles when Horizon draws your model.
Fewer triangles mean smoother performance for everyone in the world.
Turn on Statistics in the overlays to see triangle and vert counts.
The Decimate modifier cuts triangle count on a finished mesh.
Keep each single mesh under 65,535 vertices or it will not import.
lessons.tip: Pro tip: Hold detail in the texture, not the mesh. A flat wall needs only two triangles.

quiz.q: What is the vertex limit for one mesh in Horizon?

lessons.title: Export FBX For Horizon
lessons.subtitle: Send your model out the right way
steps: Select your finished object in Object Mode first.
Choose File, Export, FBX. Horizon reads the FBX format.
Turn on Selected Objects so only your model is exported.
Set the scale so the FBX comes out in meters, matching Horizon.
Apply scale and rotation before exporting to avoid odd sizing.
Save textures as PNG, power of two, 1024 pixels at most.
lessons.tip: Pro tip: Keep a tidy folder. Horizon wants the FBX plus its PNG textures together.

quiz.q: What file format does Horizon import from Blender?

lessons.title: Horizon Naming Rules
lessons.subtitle: Name materials so Horizon reads them
steps: Horizon finds surfaces by material name, so naming must be exact.
Name materials with numerals like 1, 2, 3, one per surface type.
Add a suffix for the shader: _Unlit, _Blend, _Transparent, _Masked.
A glowing sign uses _Unlit. A see-through pane uses _Transparent.
Textures must be PNG, a power of two, and 1024 pixels at most.
No normal maps. Bake any bump or shadow detail into the color map.
lessons.tip: Pro tip: Match each texture file name to its material so Horizon pairs them on import.

quiz.q: Which suffix marks a glowing, unlit material?

lessons.title: Common Import Mistakes
lessons.subtitle: Fix these before you upload
steps: Wrong scale: the model shows up giant or tiny. Apply scale in meters.
Too many tris: keep a whole model under 399,000 triangles.
A mesh over 65,535 vertices is rejected. Split or decimate it.
Bad material names break surfaces. Use numerals plus the right suffix.
Wrong textures: use PNG, power of two, up to 1024, and no normal maps.
lessons.tip: Pro tip: Run scale, tris, names and textures as a checklist every single export.

quiz.q: What is the triangle limit for a whole Horizon model?
